title: Vector Indexes: Exact, IVF and HNSW
summary: Comparing a query with every stored vector costs O(N·d) and stops being viable around millions of vectors. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (IVF, HNSW, product quantisation) trade a little recall for orders of magnitude in speed and memory. This lesson works out the costs and how to tune them.
objectives: Compute the time and memory cost of exact nearest-neighbour search for N vectors of dimension d
Explain how IVF partitions space and what nlist and nprobe trade off, with a worked scan count
Explain HNSW's layered graph, why search is roughly logarithmic, and what M and efSearch control
Compute the memory saving of product quantisation and describe its accuracy cost
Tune an index against a recall target, a latency budget and a memory budget, including the effect of metadata filters
prerequisites: You should understand embeddings and cosine similarity ([Term-Based and Embedding Retrieval](/learn/retrieval-and-rag/sparse-and-dense)) and the offline and online pipelines of [How RAG Works](/learn/retrieval-and-rag/rag-architecture). Big-O notation and bytes-per-number arithmetic are used.
